commit_reviews.summary: The greenfield SSG scaffold matches the session's tech stack (marked/gray-matter/jest) but introduces real debt — 67 naming violations, 30.3% duplication, and a premature cache-manager module that belongs to Session 5 — while wiping the entire 200-line seed baseline.

problems.description: 67 naming-convention violations (functions/classes/interfaces should be camelCase/PascalCase, constants UPPER_CASE) concentrated in cache-manager.ts and cache-manager.test.ts; measured convention score 0.46.
SonarQube delta: +7 code smells, +8 cognitive complexity, +7.5% duplication introduced across the change.

Commit scope spans +12 files for a single feature addition (templatesDir); the cache-manager surface appears unrelated to the handlebars templating feature, suggesting scope creep within the story session.

handlebars promoted from transitive devDependency to a direct runtime dependency; correct for a templating feature, but it pulls minimist/neo-async/source-map/uglify-js/wordwrap into the runtime graph — fine, just note the larger install surface.

strengths: Templating (handlebars) is an architecturally appropriate addition for a static site generator, exposed via a config-driven templatesDir option consistent with the existing contentDir/outputDir design.
All existing constructor call sites in ssg.test.ts were updated consistently to pass templatesDir, preserving the test pattern rather than breaking callers.
package-lock.json changes are consistent with the package.json edit, correctly un-marking handlebars and its transitive deps as dev-only.
commit_reviews.summary: The handlebars templating feature is architecturally sound and pattern-consistent in the visible diff, but the mechanical measurements reveal heavy convention debt (67 naming violations, convention score 0.46) and increased complexity/duplication that make the commit worse than the pre-existing state; note that the visible diff alone looks cleaner than the measurements indicate, since the bulk of the violations live in cache-manager files not shown in the excerpt.

problems.description: `notifyClients(message: any)` and `enableLiveReload((message: any) => void)` erase type safety — a `LiveReloadMessage`/`PluginMessage` type would preserve the payload contract through the callback bridge.

Mechanical convention score is 0.46 with 67 violations, but every listed violation is attributed to cache-manager.ts / cache-manager.test.ts — files not visible in this diff. Either they are pre-existing and unrelated to this commit, or the diff is truncated to hide changes there; the new plugin files (plugin.ts, plugin-manager.ts, dev-server.plugin.ts) are convention-compliant by inspection. Flagged discrepancy between qualitative review and the measurement.

SonarQube delta shows +10 smells and +23 cognitive complexity from the new plugin machinery; the ad-hoc enableLiveReload bridge (DevServer injects its notifier into the generator's plugin) couples the lifecycle to WebSocket concerns rather than emitting through the PluginContext.
Barrel re-export `PluginContext as PluginConfig` is a confusing naming alias for the public API surface.

strengths: Extracts the cohesive live-reload concern (script injection + client notification) into a dedicated plugin, shrinking dev-server.ts to HTTP/WebSocket orchestration.
Reduces duplication 3.2% by removing the inline injectLiveReloadScript from the server and delegating to the plugin.
Adds a clean extension seam — onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd lifecycle hooks — consistent with the existing markdown/template plugin naming.
Introduces a barrel export (src/index.ts) giving consumers a single public API surface.
PluginManager iteration pattern is simple and reads cleanly.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid modularity refactor that extracts live reload into a plugin system and cuts duplication, though the convention violations measured by static analysis appear to live in cache-manager files outside this diff — a discrepancy from the visible (compliant) new files — and the `any`-typed callback bridge plus +10 smells/+23 cognitive complexity add minor follow-up debt.

problems.description: CacheManager is a generic cross-cutting cache but hardcodes SSG template-engine conventions: it builds template paths as `${templateName}.hbs` and `layouts/${layoutName}.hbs` (shouldRebuildDueToTemplate/updateEntry, cache-manager.ts:83-84,94-95). A cache layer should not know the template engine's file naming — this couples a supposedly generic concern to the template engine and degrades silently (hash mismatch → rebuild) if that convention changes.

Caching is hardwired into the generator core (new CacheManager(...) in the StaticSiteGenerator constructor, ssg.ts) as a mandatory collaborator instead of being composed via the existing plugin system or dependency injection — it cannot be swapped or disabled independently of core.

'should not rebuild if file hash matches cache' passes vacuously: the source path (test/fixtures/content/hello-world.md) does not exist, so getFileHash returns '' on both update and re-check and '' === '' yields false rebuild without ever exercising a real file hash.
New module is not re-exported in src/index.ts while every other collaborator is (StaticSiteGenerator, DevServer, Plugin, PluginManager, plugins) — inconsistent public surface for the new export.

Cache manifest (.ssg-cache.json) is persisted into the output dir alongside build artifacts, and save(stats?) overloads stats bookkeeping into a persistence method, mixing responsibilities in one class.

Mechanical analyzer reports 67 naming-convention violations and convention score 0.46 (camelCase/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE), but the visible code is consistently camelCase methods, PascalCase classes/interfaces, and camelCase consts — matching existing modules (ssg.ts, plugin.ts, ssg.test.ts). The low convention score appears to be an analyzer false positive / mismatched profile; flagged per instructions as a discrepancy between measurement and qualitative judgment.

strengths: Comprehensive test coverage (218 lines) for a small module: corrupt-manifest fallback, source/template/layout change detection, persistence, clear, and stats are all exercised.
Well-scoped cross-cutting feature with cohesive integration: wired through the generator build flow and exposed via a CLI --incremental flag.

Follows existing codebase patterns closely — same import style, constructor-injected collaborator (mirrors PluginManager/MarkdownPlugin), and the same __dirname-based fixture + beforeEach/afterEach cleanup test shape as ssg.test.ts.
Graceful degradation on corrupted cache (falls back to an empty manifest rather than crashing).
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-tested incremental-build cache with reasonable integration, but it couples a generic cache to template-engine path conventions and hardwires into core rather than the plugin surface — and the reported 0.46 convention score contradicts the visibly convention-clean diff (discrepancy flagged).

compounding_issues: Session 2's hand-rolled regex Handlebars/EJS renderer (chosen over the handlebars/ejs packages) only emulates a subset of the syntax — no else/unless, @index, or nested #if/#each (non-greedy `[\s\S]*?` block regex breaks on nesting) — and this limited engine became the load-bearing template layer that Session 4 had to extract and Session 5 must hash
Session 5's incremental cache couples to arbitrary plugins: cached pages skip the onFile hook entirely, so a custom plugin with per-file side effects would silently not re-run on cache hits
The cache manifest (.ssg-cache.json) is written inside the output directory, so `--clean` wipes the very cache it needs — a deliberate but surprising coupling that survives to the final commit

The seeded baseline was discarded wholesale in Session 1 (greenfield by design), but the SSG inherited no error-handling conventions from it — malformed frontmatter/templates simply throw uncaught errors into the CLI's generic catch
key_decisions: Session 1 greenfield replaced the Express/Todo seed with a markdown→HTML SSG core (gray-matter + marked), a build CLI, and a Jest/ts-jest scaffold in a single commit
Frontmatter-driven template/layout selection: pages declare `template` and `layout`, with default fallbacks and a partials directory (Session 2)
Hand-rolled regex Handlebars/EJS renderer to avoid template-engine dependencies (Session 2)
Live-reload dev server built on chokidar + ws with serialized rebuilds (promise chaining), live-reload script injection, and a path-traversal guard on static serving (Session 3)
Full plugin architecture with onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd lifecycle hooks — markdown, template, and the dev server all become plugins, loaded via ssg.config.ts (Session 4)
Incremental builds via per-source SHA-256 hashing, whole-template-tree hash invalidation, and a .ssg-cache.json manifest (Session 5)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 establishes a clean, typed core with a working test; Session 2 layers templating on top without breaking the pipeline; Session 3 integrates a full dev server with rebuild serialization and security-aware static serving (its 3 retries show integration friction, but it lands 2/2 tests passing); Session 4 is the pivotal re-architecture, shrinking ssg.ts from ~256 lines to a thin lifecycle orchestrator by extracting markdown, template, and dev-server behavior into plugins while keeping 2/2 tests green; Session 5 adds content-hashed incremental builds and cache invalidation with 3/3 passing tests. Test coverage grew 1→1→2→2→3 with zero failures across all five sessions, exit codes were 0 throughout, and per-session cost rose (≈0.012→0.053) in step with the growing context — a signal of increasingly careful, context-heavy work rather than degradation. The one soft spot is that the S2 template engine's known limitations were carried forward rather than fixed during the S4 refactor.
story_review.summary: A coherent, well-sequenced story in which the agent built a markdown SSG core, templating, a live-reload dev server, and finally a plugin architecture with incremental caching — each session extending rather than reworking its predecessors, with tests passing and quality improving at every step.
